title: Maestral Country: Sailing and Sea-Kayaking Central Dalmatia
subRegion: Central Dalmatia, Split, Brač, Hvar & the Pakleni Islands, Vis, Šolta

bestPeriod.window: Late May-late June and early September-early October, reliable maestral, warm sea, no August berth war
bestPeriod.avoid: November-March, bura season, most island restaurants and the Blue Cave transfer service shut, and charter fleets are hauled out
bestPeriod.raw: Late May-late June and early September-early October, reliable maestral, warm sea, no August berth war

accommodation.note: Bareboat share (4 pax on a 45 ft) €550, €950, or land-based hotels €90, €180/night double

food.note: Konoba mains €14, €26, Hvar town markup 30-50%, provisioning at Tommy Split cuts this hard

transport.note: Ferries, taxi boats, Split airport transfer, car hire for the Brač days

activities.note: Marina berths, Blue Cave entry, Kornati park ticket, guided kayak days, windsurf rental

profile.difficultyNote: 3/5, sailing is low-effort, but two kayak days of 14-18 km on open water with afternoon chop is a real day out

gatewayAirport: SPU Split, 25 min to ACI Marina Split and 30 min to ACI Marina Trogir; ferry Split-Supetar (Brač) 50 min
summary: Central Dalmatia's afternoon is a machine. From roughly 11:00 the maestral fills from the northwest, builds through the early afternoon, holds 12-20 knots until about 17:00 and then switches off with the sun, which means every sailing leg, every kayak crossing and every windsurf session in this week has the same window and the same deadline. The trip is built around that: mornings on flat glass for kayaking, snorkelling and the Blue Cave, afternoons under sail or on a board. You move Split-Šolta-Vis-Hvar-Pakleni-Brač-Trogir, either on a bareboat if someone in the party holds a skipper's ticket and an SRC, or as a land-based version stitched together with car ferries and taxi boats. It suits competent, organised people who like a plan with a clock in it.

itinerary.title: Split, provisioning, and the shakedown to Šolta
itinerary.morning: Land at SPU and go straight to ACI Marina Split or ACI Trogir for the charter check-in. Present originals, skipper's ticket and SRC, and walk the boat with the base engineer properly: through-hulls, bilge pump, anchor windlass counter, tender outboard, and the location of the second reef. Land-based travellers instead check into Split and book the Šolta ferry.
itinerary.afternoon: Provision at the big Tommy or Konzum near the marina rather than on the islands, where the same basket costs 40% more. Sail out on the first of the maestral through the Split gate and cross to Šolta, anchoring in Šešula bay, deep, sheltered, thick mud holding.
itinerary.evening: Konoba Šišmiš at Šešula, on the water at the head of the bay, with a dinghy dock. Order the peka if you call ahead, it takes three hours and cannot be ordered on arrival.
itinerary.dayStats: Split-Šešula roughly 11 nm / maestral fills 11:00-13:00, 12-18 knots by mid-afternoon / Šešula anchor in 8-12 m over mud / peka must be ordered 3 h ahead
itinerary.sleep: At anchor, Šešula bay, Šolta, or Hotel Martinis Marchi, Maslinica

itinerary.title: The crossing to Vis and Komiža
itinerary.morning: Early departure while the sea is glass. The Šolta-Vis crossing is open water and best done before the maestral has any chop in it. Round the north coast of Vis to Vis town or continue west to Komiža under the flank of Hum.
itinerary.afternoon: Komiža is the working fishing town and the Blue Cave departure point. Walk the harbour, look at the *falkuša* fishing boats in the Fishermen's Museum in the Venetian tower, then swim off Kamenica beach. Divers: the Komiža centres run the *Teti* wreck and the B-17 bomber.
itinerary.evening: Konoba Jastožera in Komiža, built over the old lobster pens with the sea running under the floor. Order lobster with pasta if the budget allows, or the fish stew if it does not.
itinerary.dayStats: Šolta-Vis roughly 22-25 nm / Komiža town quay or Vis ACI marina, roughly €9.50, €11.50/m/day for a monohull / crossing best before 11:00
itinerary.sleep: At anchor or on the quay, Komiža, or Hotel San Giorgio, Vis town

itinerary.title: Biševo, the Blue Cave, and Stiniva
itinerary.morning: Biševo early. The Blue Cave's light peaks between about 11:00 and 12:00, and the queue at Mezuporat is worst from 11:30, so aim to be there by 10:00. No private boat enters the cave, the entrance is roughly 1.5 m by 2.5 m, so you buy a ticket at the Mezuporat jetty and transfer into a small licensed dinghy for a five-to-ten-minute circuit inside. Bring cash.
itinerary.afternoon: Sail back around the south coast of Vis to Stiniva, the pebble cove behind its rock gate. Boats hold off outside; swim or dinghy in. Then the Green Cave at Ravnik, which you can actually swim into, and where the light comes through a hole in the roof.
itinerary.evening: Return to Vis town and eat at Pojoda, in a courtyard of orange trees behind the waterfront, old-school Dalmatian, and the best cooking on the island.
itinerary.dayStats: Blue Cave entry ~€24 high season / ~€18 shoulder, cash only, no ATM on Biševo / cave open roughly 1 April-1 November, closed on southerly swell / peak light 11:00-12:00 / taxi boat from Komiža ~€35 pp, 15-20 min
itinerary.sleep: Vis town, at anchor or on the ACI quay

itinerary.title: Vis to Hvar and the Pakleni islands
itinerary.morning: Depart Vis on the first breeze for the run northeast to the Pakleni archipelago. This is the week's best sailing leg: 18-20 nm with a building maestral on the beam.
itinerary.afternoon: Berth at ACI Marina Palmižana on Sv. Klement or anchor off Vinogradišće on the island's sheltered south side. Palmižana bay is north-facing and exposed to any bura, so check the forecast before committing to an anchor there overnight.
itinerary.evening: Taxi boat into Hvar town, they run until late and cost a few euros. Eat at Konoba Menego in the stepped lanes above the square, then walk up to the Fortica for the view back over the Pakleni. **Plan B if jugo is forecast:** skip Hvar town, stay on the protected south side, and eat at Toto's or Laganini on Vinogradišće.
itinerary.dayStats: Vis-Palmižana roughly 18-20 nm / ACI Palmižana premium berth, budget €130, €200/night for a 13 m monohull in August / Hvar taxi boat runs to ~01:00 in season / Fortica climb 20 min, roughly €10

itinerary.title: Sea-kayaking the Pakleni archipelago
itinerary.morning: The kayak day, and it must be a morning. Launch from Palmižana or from Hvar town and thread the channels of the archipelago, Sv. Klement, Marinkovac, Jerolim, Stipanska, on flat water with 15-20 m visibility over white sand and seagrass. Guided groups typically cover 12-16 km with two swim stops.
itinerary.afternoon: Off the water before the maestral has the channels white-capping. Snorkel the shallow ledges off Jerolim, then a long lunch at Palmižana. The gardens above the bay were planted by the Meneghello family in the 1900s and are worth the walk.
itinerary.evening: Back into Hvar town for the Franciscan monastery and Zoraić or Gariful on the harbour. **Plan B if wind is up:** stay island-side; the guided kayak operators cancel above about 15 knots and will move you to the following morning.
itinerary.dayStats: Pakleni kayak day 12-16 km / guided day €70, €110 pp with boat, spray deck, dry bag and lunch / visibility typically 15-20 m / operators cancel above ~15 knots

itinerary.title: Bol, Zlatni Rat and the channel's afternoon
itinerary.morning: Cross the Hvar channel north to Bol on Brač. This is the compression zone: expect 4-8 knots more than the open-water forecast once you are in the channel, and expect it earlier in the day than elsewhere. Berth in Bol's small marina or take a mooring off Borak.
itinerary.afternoon: The reason you came. Rig at Big Blue Sport on Beach Borak, immediately west of the Zlatni Rat spit, side-shore maestral, pebble bottom, flat inshore water and short chop outside. If the wind is under 12 knots, take their sea kayak or SUP option and paddle west along the cliffs instead.
itinerary.evening: Konoba Mlin in Bol, in an old olive mill in the back lanes. Order the lamb and ask for a Brač Plavac Mali. **Plan B for a windless afternoon:** drive or taxi up to the Blaca hermitage, a 15th-century monastery in a gorge, reachable only on foot for the last kilometre.
itinerary.dayStats: Hvar channel crossing 8-10 nm / Big Blue Sport funboard ~€50/hour or ~€310/week; beginner course ~€200 for 6 hours; private advanced ~€140/hour / board storage €5, €7/day / Bol channel adds 4-8 knots
itinerary.sleep: Hotel Kaštil, Bol, or at anchor off Borak

itinerary.title: Milna, Trogir and the hand-back
itinerary.morning: Sail west along the south coast of Brač and round to Milna, or run straight for the base. If you are still hungry for one more open-water leg and the maestral is early, the Kornati day-sail option leaves from further north and needs a full day plus a park ticket, treat it as an add-on rather than a day-seven squeeze.
itinerary.afternoon: Return the boat at ACI Trogir or ACI Split. Trogir is the better hand-back because the UNESCO old town is a five-minute walk over the bridge and you can spend the dead hours in the Cathedral of St Lawrence looking at Radovan's 1240 portal instead of in a marina car park.
itinerary.evening: Konoba Trs in Trogir, in a stone courtyard off the main lane. Then a last walk on the Riva.
itinerary.dayStats: Bol-Trogir roughly 26-30 nm / hand-back typically 09:00 with a fuel and damage inspection / Kornati one-day boat ticket for 11-17.99 m roughly €95 in season bought in advance, about double on-site
itinerary.sleep: Hotel Bellevue or Palace Derossi, Trogir, or an airport hotel

accommodationStrategy.name: The bareboat itself
accommodationStrategy.location: 42-47 ft monohull from ACI Split or ACI Trogir
accommodationStrategy.description: Sleeping aboard is what makes the itinerary work: you are already at the anchorage when the light is right at Stiniva and the Blue Cave, and you skip the ferry timetable entirely. A 45 ft four-cabin monohull in June runs roughly €3,200, €4,800 a week plus a transit log of €100, €200 and berthing, which lands at €550, €950 per person for a full boat. Requires a skipper's ticket and an SRC in the crew.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Kaštil
accommodationStrategy.location: 15th-century stone building on the Bol waterfront
accommodationStrategy.description: The land-based anchor for the Brač days. Directly on the harbour and a ten-minute walk along the seafront promenade to Beach Borak and Big Blue Sport, so you can carry a rig if you have to and check the channel from the terrace. Roughly €140, €230 double B&B in season.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Martinis Marchi
accommodationStrategy.style: restored 18th-century castle with its own small marina
accommodationStrategy.description: The one splurge, and the only place on Šolta with a proper berth attached to a hotel room. Useful as a first or last night if you are land-based, because Šolta is 50 minutes from Split by ferry and feels an order of magnitude quieter than Hvar. Roughly €260, €420 double.

logistics.connectivity: 4G is good along the whole coast and in every town on this route; it drops in the lee of Vis's Hum and inside the Pakleni channels. Croatia is in the EU and Schengen, so EU roaming applies at domestic rates. Download Navionics or a chart app with offline vector charts before you leave the marina, the Pakleni are full of unmarked rock heads.
logistics.emergency: **195 for maritime search and rescue**, 112 for everything else, VHF Channel 16 monitored by MRCC Rijeka and the coastal radio stations. Split has the regional hospital (KBC Split); Hvar and Vis have health centres only, and a serious case is a helicopter or fast-boat transfer to Split. Travel insurance must name sailing and, separately, sea kayaking, many policies treat "watersports" as a bolt-on. Decompression chamber: Split.
logistics.weather: Check DHMZ (meteo.hr) and its dedicated coastal-waters forecast alongside Windy; Croatian marinas post the daily forecast at the capitanerie office. The bura arrives faster than any other Adriatic wind and its gusts are two to three times the mean, so a "35 knot bura" means 60-knot hits. The jugo announces itself a day ahead with a greasy swell from the southeast and falling pressure. Neither is a summer certainty, but both happen in June and September.
logistics.bookingWindows: Bareboats for July and August go six to nine months ahead; June and September, three to four months. Charter paperwork, skipper's ticket, SRC, crew list, sojourn tax, should be with the base four to six weeks before departure. ACI berths in Hvar, Palmižana and Trogir cannot be pre-booked cheaply and in August you should be in the marina by 15:00. Kornati tickets: buy online at the parks system in advance to halve the price. Restaurants on Hvar and Vis in August need two to three days.
logistics.money: Croatia adopted the euro on 1 January 2023, so prices are in EUR and older kuna price lists you find online are historic. Cards work in towns and marinas. Carry cash for the Blue Cave (cash only), taxi boats, island konobas and Biševo generally. Tipping is 10% at a sit-down meal.
logistics.transportRules: Bringing a rental car onto a car ferry needs the rental company's permission, which is usually granted for domestic island routes and refused for Bosnia and Montenegro. Jadrolinija's Split-Supetar car ferry runs roughly hourly in summer and takes 50 minutes; catamarans to Hvar and Vis are foot-passenger only. Croatian motorway tolls apply on the A1 from Zagreb; there is no vignette.
logistics.permits: National-park entry is charged per boat per day and enforced by park rangers who board. Anchoring on *Posidonia oceanica* seagrass is prohibited; anchor on sand. Inside Kornati and Telašćica, anchoring is confined to designated bays and overnight stays often require a mooring buoy. Spearfishing requires a permit and is banned in national parks and near-total for non-residents in some zones. Drones need HCAA-compliant operation and are banned over Diocletian's Palace and Trogir's old town. A vessel over 15 m or carrying more than 12 people has additional reporting duties.
logistics.health: Tap water is potable throughout Croatia including on the islands, though tanked marina water is best filtered. Sea urchins are the dominant injury, the entire coast is rock and pebble. The weever fish (*Trachinus*) buries in sand in shallow water and its spine hurts badly; hot-water immersion is the treatment. Sunburn on a boat is systematically underestimated because the maestral cools you. No sharks worth thinking about and no dangerous jellyfish.

proTips: Get your SRC before you get excited about the boat. Croatia enforces the VHF radio operator's certificate as hard as the skipper's ticket, it is the requirement most crews discover four weeks out, and no charter base will hand over keys without the original.
Every long crossing goes in the morning. The maestral means the sea is glass at 08:00 and choppy at 15:00, so a Vis crossing planned for after lunch is a crossing planned badly.
Buy the Kornati boat ticket online before you sail. Bought at a ranger's boat inside the park it is roughly double, and rangers do board.

Arrive at Mezuporat on Biševo by 10:00 with cash. The light in the Blue Cave peaks 11:00-12:00 and the queue peaks 11:30, those two facts are why the trip so often disappoints, and why arriving an hour early fixes it.
Take a berth by 15:00 in July and August, or plan to anchor. Palmižana, Hvar and Trogir fill in the late afternoon and there is no reservation system that reliably saves you.
Provision in Split, not on the islands. A trolley at the big Tommy near ACI Split is 30-40% cheaper than the same trolley in Hvar town, and island shops close for a long lunch.
Order peka three hours ahead. Every konoba on this route will make it and none will make it on demand, a phone call from the anchorage at midday is the difference.

At Bol, ride the channel edge rather than the beach edge. The compression between Brač and Hvar means the wind five hundred metres out is meaningfully stronger and cleaner than the wind at the launch, and the pebble spit's tip genuinely moves with the season.
Keep one flexible day in the middle of the week. Jugo and bura both cost a day when they come, and a week with no slack turns a weather event into a cancelled Blue Cave you have paid for.

raw.Prevailing wind, the maestral (also *mae: a thermal northwesterly generated by the temperature difference between the heated Dalmatian hinterland and the cooler sea. It is the summer wind and the reason this coast works. Typical cycle: nothing at 08:00, first ripples 10:30-11:30, 8-12 knots by 13:00, peak 12-20 knots from 14:00 to 17:00, easing from 18:00 and gone by sunset. Occasional 22-25 knot days in June and September. It is strongest and most reliable in the channels, the Bol channel between Brač and Hvar and the Split gate, where compression adds 4-8 knots over open water. This is exactly why Bol is the Adriatic's windsurf capital.
raw.The two winds that end the plan, bura an: the *bura* (bora) is a dry, cold, brutally gusty northeasterly that falls off the Dinaric wall. Its season is October to April but summer episodes happen, usually 12-36 hours, arriving fast, gusting to 40-60 knots in the accelerating gaps (Velebit channel, the Vrulja gap on the Makarska riviera, the Split channel) and leaving a hard blue sky behind it. Bura gusts are the reason charter contracts forbid certain anchorages. The *jugo* (sirocco) is the opposite personality: a warm, humid southeasterly that builds slowly over a day or more, brings low cloud and rain, and, crucially, builds real swell, 1.5-3 m in the open channels. Jugo is what closes the Blue Cave and cancels catamaran ferries. A third, the *levanat* easterly, is short-lived and mostly a nuisance.
raw.Launch spots and sailing water: *Zlatni Rat / Beach Borak, Bol (Brač)*, the famous shifting shingle spit; the windsurf launch is off Borak beach immediately west, side-shore maestral, smooth pebble bottom, flat inshore water building to short chop, superb for intermediates, with the hazard being the Bol channel current and the fact that the spit's tip and the water depth around it move. *Šešula bay, Šolta*, deep, protected, thick holding mud, the archetypal first-night anchorage. *Stiniva, Vis*, a pebble cove behind a 10 m rock gate, no anchoring inside, boats hold off; the swim in is the point. *Palmižana bay, Sv. Klement (Pakleni)*, north-facing, sand and seagrass, exposed to bura, home to ACI Marina Palmižana. *Vinogradišće* on the same island's south side, the kayak lunch stop. *Jerolim and Stipanska*, the inner Pakleni, flat, sheltered, 10 minutes by taxi boat from Hvar town.
raw.Equipment hubs and certification: *Big Blue Sport* on Beach Borak at Bol is the anchor operation, VDWS-affiliated, running roughly 40 Flikka boards and 60 Severne rigs plus sea-kayak, SUP and mountain-bike programmes, with a café and shop on the beach. Indicative rates: beginner windsurf course €200 for 6 hours, advanced private tuition around €140/hour, school-board rental from about €25/hour, funboard about €50/hour or €310 for the week, board storage €5, €7 per day and rig storage €5, €8. For kayaking, Split-based operators run the Pakleni archipelago and the Split-Čiovo coast as guided day trips at roughly €70, €110 per person including boat, spray deck, dry bag and lunch. Diving is PADI and SSI both, centres cluster at Komiža (Vis), Hvar town and Bol.
raw.Tides, the honest number: Central Dalmatia is near-tideless. Spring range at Split is roughly 0.3-0.5 m and neaps under 0.2 m; the northern Adriatic around Venice reaches a metre or so, but you are not there. There are no tidal gates, no tide-dependent breaks and no reason to consult a tide table for a launch. What *does* move the water is meteorological: a strong jugo can pile 0.3-0.5 m of water into the bays on top of the astronomical tide, and a hard bura pushes it back out. Currents are weak, generally under 1 knot, running broadly northwest along the coast, but they accelerate around headlands and through the narrow channels, and the Bol channel and the Split gate both reward a look at the water before a kayak crossing.
raw.Sea conditions and safety: water temperature runs roughly 17-19°C in May, 22-23°C in June, 24-25°C in July, 25-26°C in August, 23-24°C in September and 20-21°C in October. June to September needs nothing more than a lycra for a session; May and October justify a 3/2 shorty for windsurfing and a light top for kayaking, because the maestral is cooling even when the sea is warm. Jellyfish are a minor issue, occasional *Pelagia noctiluca* and the harmless fried-egg *Cotylorhiza*. Sea urchins are the real hazard and Dalmatian pebble-and-rock entries are full of them; reef shoes on every rocky entry, without exception. Lifeguards exist on the main managed beaches (Zlatni Rat, Bačvice) in July and August and nowhere else. **Croatian search and rescue at sea: 195. General emergency: 112.** MRCC Rijeka coordinates; VHF Channel 16 is monitored.
raw.Bareboat charter, the licence and the pa: Croatia requires at least one person aboard with a recognised skipper's qualification **and** a VHF radio operator's certificate, SRC, LRC or GMDSS. The VHF certificate is the requirement people forget and it is strictly enforced by the harbourmaster and coastguard; photocopies are not accepted, originals only. RYA Day Skipper and an ICC for coastal waters are both recognised, alongside qualifications from the many countries with which the Croatian ministry has bilateral recognition. Expect to submit documents four to six weeks before the charter, to pay a transit log of roughly €100, €200, and to file a crew list, the Croatian system requires the crew list and sojourn tax to be lodged electronically before departure, and the charter base normally does this for you. Charter companies typically also want a logbook showing five to fifteen documented sailing days depending on yacht size.
raw.Marina and park fees: ACI marina daily berthing for a 10-20 m monohull averages roughly €9.50, €11.50 per metre per day, with ACI Split, ACI Trogir and ACI Palmižana at the expensive end of the network; catamarans run 50-100% more, around €16.50, €20.50 per metre. Budget €130, €200 a night for a 13 m monohull at a premium Central Dalmatian ACI berth in August, less in June. National-park entry is charged per boat per day: for an 11.00-17.99 m vessel, Kornati is roughly €95 in peak season (June-September) and €50 outside it when bought in advance, bought inside the park at a mobile reception desk it is around double, so buy online. Kornati tickets run 00:00-24:00 and stay valid until 12:00 the next day. The Blue Cave at Biševo charges roughly €24 per adult in high season (about 20 June-10 September) and €18 in shoulder season, cash only at the island, with no ATM.
raw.Weather-contingency plan: *No maestral*, this is the good problem. Use it: kayak the Pakleni channels on glass, dive or freedive the Green Cave at Ravnik, motor to Stiniva, do the Blue Cave in the 10:30-13:00 light window. *Jugo*, get to a protected marina early, because everyone else will want the same berth by 16:00; the Blue Cave closes on southerly swell even under a clear sky, and ferry catamarans cancel before the big car ferries do. *Bura*, do not cross channels; stay put, and if you are on a bareboat, expect the charter base to phone you with instructions rather than the other way round. Land alternatives: Diocletian's Palace and the Split cellars, Trogir's Radovan portal, the Blaca hermitage on Brač, and Vis's Tito's Cave and the abandoned military tunnels.

sources.confidenceNotes: Marina rates vary by month and by exact length band, confirm the specific ACI tariff for your boat and dates. Charter prices for a 45 ft monohull are indicative market figures, not quotes. Blue Cave season dates and the exact high-season window shift year to year and the cave closes at short notice on swell; re-verify before publishing. Kayak day-trip prices and the ~15-knot cancellation threshold are operator-dependent. Restaurant status on Vis, Šolta and the Pakleni changes between seasons, Jastožera, Pojoda, Šišmiš, Menego, Mlin and Trs should each be re-checked for 2026 opening. Distances in nautical miles are planning approximations from chart, not measured routes. Croatia's national SAR number 195 and MRCC Rijeka coordination should be confirmed against the current official listing. The maestral figures are climatological norms; June and September deliver it less reliably than July and August even though they are better months to travel.
